Title: DEFENDING THE INTERNET OF MEDICAL THINGS (IOMT): A KUBERNETES-ORCHESTRATED DEEP LEARNING FRAMEWORK FOR ZERO-DAY THREAT DETECTION IN MEDICAL ELECTRONICS
Author: Joya Qureshi|Pratishtha Singh|Aamir Abdullah Khan|Aliza Bano|Yasharth Shekhar
Abstract: Medical devices that connect to the internet now multiply at high speed and this growth changes everyday care. Insulin pumps and brain linked chips send plus receive data through radio links - physicians watch patients from a distance in real time. But the same radio paths give attackers a way to reach the implants. Batteries inside the body remain tiny - the implants lack the energy for standard encryption or virus scanners. The study presents a cloud style security plan that moves all heavy defense work off the implant and into an edge network owned by the hospital. A cluster of small servers near patient wards runs under Kubernetes control. Each server hosts a detector built from a Long Short Term Memory Autoencoder, a kind of neural net that learns normal traffic and flags deviations. A passive mirror port copies every packet that leaves or reaches the implants - the copy streams through the detector - no extra load drains the implanted battery. Kubernetes keeps the detector online even when part of the cluster fails, adds more pods during a sudden flood of traffic but also rolls out new threat profiles without manual steps. Simulated attacks show the system spots unknown exploits with high accuracy while the added delay stays below one thousandth of a second.

Title: Pre-Symptomatic Prediction of Fusarium Wilt Tropical Race 4 in Banana Plantations via Multispectral Unmanned Aerial Vehicles Imagery and Edaphic Data Fusion
Author: Mayank Namdev|Abhishek Singh Rathore|Amol Dhumane|Rahul A. Patil|Geeta S. Navale|Dattatray G. Takale|Ashish Mishra|Vipin Tiwari
Abstract: Hybrid Convolutional Neural Network Multilayer Perceptron model integrates multispectral Unmanned Aerial Vehicles imagery and soil data for early, pre-symptomatic Fusarium wilt prediction with actionable risk mapping.

Title: Computational evaluation of tentatively identified phytochemicals from pine needle aqueous extract and their predicted ACE2-binding interactions
Author: PRIYA KAUSHIK|Ashwani Mathur
Abstract: Pine needles are a rich but underexplored source of phytochemicals. This study combined LC-MS profiling and computational approaches to investigate compounds tentatively identified from pine needle aqueous extract and their predicted interactions with angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2; PDB ID: 1R4L). Molecular docking was performed using MLN-4760 as a reference ligand. Embelin, a synthetic Pyrrolo[3,4-c]pyrazole derivative, DL-Carbidopa, Thymidine, and D-pantothenic acid showed docking affinities of -9.601, -9.367, -7.073, -7.064, and -5.796 kcal/mol, respectively, compared with -7.654 kcal/mol for MLN-4760. Drug-likeness, pharmacokinetic, and toxicity properties were evaluated using SwissADME and PubChem. Molecular dynamics simulation was used to further examine the top-ranked compound, Embelin. Throughout the simulation, the ACE2-Embelin complex showed limited structural fluctuation and persistent interactions within the binding pocket. MMAPBSA analysis yielded a binding free energy of -18.52 kcal/mol, indicating favorable protein-ligand association. Additionally, the majority of compounds showed acceptable expected pharmacokinetic profiles and met important drug-likeness criteria. Thus, the study shows the usefulness of integration computational screening with LC-MS analysis to find potential phytochemicals from pine needles and predict ACE2 binding potential. To confirm these results and ascertain their biological significance, more biological research is needed.

Title: Secrecy outage and capacity analysis for UAV-assisted IRS-aided G2G system
Author: Nikita Goel|Pankaj Kumar|Sandesh Jain|Manoj Tolani|Swati Varun Yadav|Sam Darshi
Abstract: The integration of intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) with unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) is rapidly emerging as a groundbreaking approach to enhancing the performance of 5G and beyond (5G+) wireless networks. This paper considers UAV-assisted-IRS-aided ground-to-ground (G2G) communication (UA-IRS-G2G) for improving the reliability of ground users (GUs) in infrastructure-less scenarios. To develop the mathematical framework for UA-IRS-G2G system, a height-dependent Nakagami- m fading channel is assumed for the IRS-to-GU links, while a Rayleigh fading channel is adopted for the G2G links, accounting for the multipath effect between the GUs. For the same, the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the end-to-end signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for signals transmitted via UA-IRS is derived. Furthermore, the closed-form expressions of secrecy outage probability (SOP) and secrecy capacity are also derived for the considered scenario. Additionally, diversity order is employed to enhance the reliability of the received signal at the receiver node in the proposed scenario. At the end numerical simulations are conducted to validate the accuracy of these theoretical derivations. The performance of the proposed work is compared with the existing state-of-the-art method reported in 11 . The results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves better performance than the existing method in 11 .

Title: Controlled high-harmonic generation using two-color laser fields for isolated attosecond pulse generation in argon
Author: Sumit Kumar|Sandeep Kumar|Prashant Chauhan|Shruti Gulihar|Niti Kant|Mukesh Jewaria
Abstract: Isolated attosecond pulses with broad spectral range provide a powerful tool for probing ultra-fast studies in atoms and molecules. In this study, we report two-color laser field control on high-harmonic generation (HHG) in argon for attosecond pulse generation. Two-color laser fields are synthesized by keeping the wavelength of the first laser fixed while varying the second laser. In HHG, the harmonic cut-off and synthesis of an isolated attosecond pulse are strongly dependent on the electric field waveform, laser pulse duration, the time delays between the two lasers, the carrier–envelope phase (CEP) of the laser, and laser intensities. The use of two-color driving fields enables extending the harmonic cut-off to the water window region, which offers better control over the microscopic electron dynamics and flexibility of tuning compared to single-laser HHG. Our study demonstrates an isolated attosecond pulse with 345 eV energy and 449 attosecond full width at half-maximum (FWHM) pulse width for −1.2fs time delay between the two lasers of 5 fs FWHM each. For ΔCEP=3 π /2, an isolated attosecond pulse with a pulse width of 340 attosecond FWHM is obtained with a cut-off photon energy of 367 eV. These ultra-short pulses will be highly beneficial for investigating the electron dynamics study inside atoms, molecules, solids, and other systems, where fundamental processes occur on the attosecond timescale.

Title: Genome-Wide Mitochondrial Heteroplasmy Reveals Predominantly Individual-Specific Variation in Indian Indigenous Cattle
Author: Manisha Sharma|Rahul Shrivastava|Ramesh Kumar Vijh
Abstract: Mitochondrial heteroplasmy is a prominent source of intra-individual genetic variation. However, their genome-wide and population-level structure remains insufficiently characterized in livestock. This study considers complete mitochondrial genome sequences (16341 bp) from 46 indigenous cattle animals representing six Indian breeds. High-quality mitochondrial variants were identified using a standardized bioinformatics pipeline that included next-generation sequencing, quality filtering, de novo assembly, and heteroplasmy detection. Out of the total, 16 indigenous cattle mitochondrial sequences exhibited heteroplasmy variation and were further investigated to assess their distribution across individuals, populations, and functional gene categories. A total of 245 heteroplasmic events were found across 223 unique heteroplasmic sites, with 209 (93.72%) sites restricted to individual animals. Heteroplasmic profiles demonstrated very low similarity among individuals (mean Jaccard distance = 0.990 ± 0.020), indicating high inter-individual heterogeneity. A considerable variation in heteroplasmy burden was found among individuals and breeds (Kruskal–Wallis test: individuals χ² = 70.34, P = 3.89 × 10⁻⁹; breeds χ² = 34.76, P = 1.68 × 10⁻⁶). Although no significant clustering by breed identity was observed (PERMANOVA; F = 1.011, P = 0.303). Furthermore, 76 non-synonymous and 62 synonymous heteroplasmic substitutions were detected at the functional level. However, their allele frequency distributions were not noticeably different (Wilcoxon test, P = 0.881). Gene-wise analyses show no consistent enrichment of heteroplasmic variants after multiple-testing correction. Overall, mitochondrial heteroplasmy in cattle was characterized by highly individual variation, weak population structure, and a lack of detectable functional-class differentiation at the allele-frequency level.

Title: Phytochemical profiling and heavy metal accumulation in organic and local market food crops: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) - based comparative evaluation
Author: Aditi Raj|Pammi Gauba|Ekta Bhatt
Abstract: This study explores the bioactive compounds in five vegetables, namely Indian mustard ( Brassica juncea ), lettuce ( Lactuca sativa ), spinach ( Spinacia oleracea ), cabbage ( Brassica oleracea L. var. capitata ), curry leaves ( Murraya koenigii ), one underutilized fruit, Indian gooseberry ( Phyllanthus emblica ), and one agricultural waste, rice stubble ( Oryza sativa L. ), obtained from organic sources and a local market in Ghaziabad, India, to evaluate their nutritional significance. These samples were analysed on the basis of their moisture, ash, chlorophyll, carotenoid, flavonoid, and eavy metal contents. It was observed that lettuce had the highest moisture content i.e. > 94%. Rice stubble had the highest ash content (14.26%), whereas Indian gooseberry had the lowest (< 0.9%). Organic mustard had the highest chlorophyll content i.e. 1.89 mg mL⁻¹, whereas organic curry leaves had the highest carotenoid content (0.50 mg mL⁻¹). Indian gooseberry had the highest phenolic compounds as well as flavonoid content. The study is one of the first to use a combined ICP-MS - PCA approach to jointly benchmark heavy metal and bioactive profiles across organic versus market source produce. Heavy metal concentrations in both organic and market vegetable samples were within allowable limits, confirming overall food safety. However, an integrated ICP-MS and PCA framework revealed that organic samples had a slightly lower trace elemental baseline and marginally higher bioactive compound content than market crops, with both categories remaining largely comparable in terms of composition and quality.

Title: Comparative analysis of protein content, phytochemical composition, and In-Silico characterization of EF1-α in Morchella esculenta
Author: Jyoti Dhyan|Shikha Mittal|Kritika Singh|Hemant Sood
Abstract: Morchella esculenta is a nutritious edible mushroom that contains a variety of bioactive substances. The Present study employed biochemical and bioinformatics approaches to evaluate the protein content, phytochemical composition, and molecular properties of Morchella esculenta . For protein and phytochemical analyses, Guchhi samples were processed to prepare an aqueous paste and CHAPS solution of Guchhi extracts. Compared to CHAPS Solution (12.62 mg/mL), aqueous paste had higher protein content (20.17 mg/mL). Likewise, aqueous paste had greater levels of total phenolics (8.64 mg/mL), flavonoids (10.56 mg/mL), carbohydrates (5.27 mg/mL), alkaloids (8.22 mg/mL), and antioxidant activity (8.630 mg/mL) than CHAPS Solution.Bioinformatics analysis of the elongation factor 1-alpha protein revealed a high degree of sequence similarity among homologous proteins together with conserved functional domains and characteristic protein motifs. In addition, RNA-Seq revealed 2,851 significantly differentially expressed genes between two developmental stages, including 2,596 upregulated and 255 downregulated genes. These findings provide a comprehensive biochemical and molecular characterization of Morchella esculenta and establish a foundation for future nutritional, functional, transcriptomic and comparative studies.

Title: Antioxidant Defense Mechanism in Plants Under Salt Stress: Physiological, Biochemical and Molecular Insights
Author: Apurva Ahlawat|Nivedita Mishra|Monika Bajpai
Abstract: Recent researches focus on intensive high-input agricultural practices for maximizing crop yield, involve heavy use of fertilizers, pesticides, and irrigation. These methods increase food production but often lead to environmental degradation, including soil erosion, and increased soil salinity. On the cellular level, salinity elevates the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which cause oxidative damage to lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids, and also serve as signalling molecules and trigger stress responses in plants. Plants counteract these challenges by integrating cellular, biochemical, and molecular adaptations that help to sustain cellular homeostasis. The major component of this whole mechanism is the antioxidant defense system, which consists of various enzymatic components (superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), peroxidases (POD), ascorbate peroxidase (APX), glutathione reductase (GR), and non-enzymatic antioxidants (ascorbate, glutathione, tocopherols, carotenoids, phenolics, compatible osmolytes). These systems synergize to control the ROS levels and maintain redox balance in a saline environment. Moreover, salinity stress triggers intricate networks of molecular signalling, which comprise ROS, calcium signalling, and kinase-mediated pathways. Other pathways that maintain ion homeostasis include the SOS signalling system. A combination of these mechanisms helps plants maintain metabolic stability and adapt to saline conditions. The present review aims to provide in-depth critical insights into these interdependent responses in plants to understand how they contribute to enhancing stress tolerance and improving crop productivity. Such understanding will be highly valuable for developing strategies to optimize plant responses under rising salinity levels and, consequently, improve crop yield.

Title: Optimization of Pleurotus ostreatus as a potent bioremediation agent for the removal of methylene blue dye in wastewater
Author: Bandana Thakur|Anil Kant|Ashok Kumar Nadda
Abstract: The widespread use of methylene blue (MB) as a cationic thiazine dye in the textile and chemical industries has raised environmental concerns due to its high stability against biodegradation. The persistence of MB in aquatic ecosystems is due to its complex aromatic structure and cationic nature, which make it highly resistant to natural degradation. Its persistence in water has been linked to toxic effects on living organisms and disruption of the ecological balance of aquatic ecosystems. Several methods use white rot fungi and other organisms for dye degradation, therefore becoming a hot topic of research lately. The present study is aimed at identifying the optimum conditions for the growth of Pleurotus ostreatus in terms of pH, temperature, and incubation time for maximum biomass production. The study further investigates the efficacy of the fungus, P. ostreatus , together with laccase-inducing substances such as copper sulfate, tannic acid, ethanol, Tween-80 and gallic acid, for the efficient elimination of the cationic methylene blue dye. The fungus was cultivated with different laccase inducers and varying concentrations of methylene blue dye. The extent of dye removal under different experimental treatments was evaluated based on the degree of dye decolorization. The treatment having P. ostreatus in media along with tannic acid (TA) was the most efficient in methylene blue removal, with rates as high as 99 ± 0.54%. It was also observed that P. ostreatus , along with the other inducer treatments, performed better than the control treatment at lower MB concentrations. This implies that P. ostreatus has the potential of being a reliable biosorbent and bioremediation agent in the process of textile dye removal. Also, compounds such as TA and copper sulfate may then be used to enhance its performance by stimulating its ligninolytic enzyme system.

Title: Role of conserved regions in PETase-mediated degradation
Author: Sandhya Tegta|Shikha Mittal|Jitendraa Vashistt
Abstract: Plastic pollution generated by polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is a major environmental issue due to its high stability and resistance to natural degradation. In recent years, several bacterial genus like Ideonella , Pseudomonas , Bacillus , Thermobifida , and Rhodococcus , have been reported for their ability to break down PET. An enzyme PETase has been identified in Ideonella sakaiensis which shows an important role in catalytic activity in PET degradation. It also found that PETase enzyme has a conserved region which contains catalytic amino acid triad (-SHD-) for substrate binding and enzyme stability. Previous studies have also reported the PET-degrading potential of R. pyridinivorans ; however, the molecular characteristics of its PET esterase-like proteins remain poorly understood. Therefore, to decipher the molecular details a biodegradation, a bioinformatic approach was utilized. In this study, we identified the potential PET-degrading enzymes using in silico approach. Previous studies have reported that the Abhydrolase_3 (PF07859) domain is associated with PET esterase-like proteins in R. pyridinivorans . Bioinformatic analysis revealed PET esterase-like proteins in R. pyridinivorans which contain Abhydrolase_3 domain having PETase like activity. Alpha-fold was utilized for creation of three-dimensional structure of PETase for R. pyridinivorans . Present study reveals the presence of PETase-like proteins in R. pyridinivorans , which was also confirmed at motif level evidence. The results may pave a direction in confirming the biodegradation potential of R. pyridinivorans.

Title: Comparative Phytochemical and Antimicrobial Evaluation of Rosa damascena Herrm. and Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton
Author: Priyanka Yadav|Anuj Kumar|Rachana R
Abstract: Rosa damascena Herrm. and Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton are important medicinal plants used since ancient times. These two plants are chosen for the present study to compare their bioactive potential under standardized conditions. The existing study explored the phytochemical composition, antimicrobial, antioxidant, and antifungal actions of their ethanolic extracts. Qualitative tests have shown that there were alkaloids, tannins, flavonoids, saponins, cardiac glycosides, triterpenoids, and phenols in both species. Quantitative analysis showed that R. damascena exhibited higher phenolic content (35.98 ± 0.06 mgGAE/g), whereas J. sambac showed higher flavonoid content (49.00 ± 0.04 mgQE/g). FTIR spectroscopy revealed characteristic functional groups associated with various phytocompounds. The extract of R. damascena demonstrated stronger antioxidant and antibacterial effects against Escherichia coli and Bacillus subtilis, as well as better antifungal activity against Aspergillus ochraceus, whereas J. sambac exhibited moderate activity. These findings establish that both these plants are promising sources of bioactive phytocompounds; advanced studies are essential to set apart active constituents with validation of their therapeutic applications.

Title: Bipolar Disorder: An Integrated Neuroscience and Neuropsychological Review
Author: Aaradhya Arora|Manisha Singh
Abstract: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a chronic and heterogeneous psychiatric condition with recurrent manic, hypomanic, and depressive episodes, and significant psychosocial dysfunction. Besides mood disturbances, converging evidence shows that cognitive, brain circuit, neurotransmission, inflammation, cellular energy metabolism and synaptic plasticity abnormalities persist. This narrative review synthesises molecular neuroscience, neuroimaging and neuropsychological studies on the possibility of biological changes and their role in cognitive and behavioural symptoms in BD. Dysfunction of prefrontal, limbic, hippocampal, anterior cingulate and associated networks has been suggested to underlie disrupted emotional processing, executive function, memory, attention and processing speed. Neurotransmitter systems such as dopamine, serotonin, glutamate and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) do not act alone but instead engage in interactions with intracellular signalling, calcium homeostasis, oxidative stress, mitochondrial function and with the neuroimmune processes. The role of neuroinflammatory and neurotrophic mechanisms in the modulation of neuronal resilience and synaptic plasticity is likely to be further modulated, but findings from biomarkers remains inconsistent depending on mood state, therapy and methodologic issues. However, improved understanding of how these mechanisms work has come from structural and functional neuroimaging, diffusion imaging, electroencephalography, and molecular approaches, but these measures are not yet clinically validated and are not suitable for use as biomarkers in routine clinical diagnosis or treatment selection. Neuropsychological assessment is also important as a complementary assessment to identify cognitive profiles that may remain before and after the acute mood phase and that may be involved in functional disability. The integration of biological and neuropsychological information then may help to inform more personalized assessment and intervention. Longitudinal studies, standardized phenotyping, multimodal studies, use of digital measures, machine learning, and validation of biomarkers in clinically diverse groups should be the focus of future research. In general, a combined neuroscience/neuropsychology approach to the study of BD may be more informative and support the individualized design of treatment plans aimed at mental functioning.

Title: Nephroprotective Potential of Tinospora cordifolia : Phytochemical Profiling and Antioxidant Protection Against Glucose-Induced Oxidative Stress
Author: S. K. Yadav|Pammi Gauba|Vibha Rani
Abstract: Diabetic nephropathy (DN), a microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus, represents a major cause of end-stage renal (ESRD) disease and is caused by hyperglycemia-induced oxidative stress and inflammation. Current therapeutic strategies offer title protection against DN, underscoring the need for more effective and targeted interventions. Tinospora cordifolia (T. cordifolia), a medicinal plant used extensively for traditional purposes, possesses strong antioxidant and nephroprotective actions. In this study, the nephroprotective action of T. cordifolia has been assessed through phytochemical analysis and its protective ability against oxidative stress induced in DN. Analysis indicated the existence of several bioactive compounds, involve glycosides, alkaloids, phenols, and flavonoids, which have proven therapeutic significance. It was found that treatment with T. cordifolia significantly reduced oxidative stress indicators such as ROS levels and lipid peroxidation, increased the activity of antioxidants, including superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase, & glutathione peroxidase. Furthermore, treatment was observed to have a beneficial effect on renal function parameters and helped reduce histopathological changes such as glomerular hypertrophy and tubular damage. On a mechanistic level, the renoprotective properties of T. cordifolia can be attributed to a balance in oxidative stress and inflammation signaling, resulting in a reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokine expression and fibrosis. From these results, it can be concluded that T. cordifolia is a promising candidate in protecting against kidney damage caused by diabetes.

Title: Comparative Evaluation of Antimicrobial and Antibiofilm Activity of Furfural in a Model Bacterial System
Author: Kajal Rawat|Reema Gabrani
Abstract: The natural compound furfural, obtained from biomass, has been investigated for its antimicrobial properties. However, its comparative antimicrobial, antibiofilm, and antibiotic-modulating activities across different bacterial species have not yet been explored. This research focused on the antimicrobial and antibiofilm effects of furfural against Acinetobacter baylyi, Pseudomonas fluorescens, and Staphylococcus epidermidis . The antibacterial activity of furfural was quantified through a broth microdilution assay, whereas antibiofilm activity was determined using the crystal violet assay. The interaction between furfural and gentamicin was evaluated by checkerboard microdilution. Furfural exhibited concentration-dependent antibacterial and antibiofilm activity across all tested microorganisms. The Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of furfural was 1000 µg/mL for all three bacteria. The Minimum biofilm inhibition concentration (MBIC) was 1000 µg/mL for A. baylyi and P. fluorescens , whereas the MBIC for S. epidermidis was 2500 µg/mL. The MIC of gentamicin was 125 µg/mL against A. baylyi and 62.5 µg/mL against S. epidermidis and P. fluorescens . Combination analysis showed synergy against P. fluorescens (FICI = 0.5), an additive effect against A. baylyi (FICI = 1.0), and S. epidermidis (FICI = 0.75). These findings indicate that furfural exhibits antimicrobial, antibiofilm activities and species-dependent interactions with gentamicin, providing a basis for further evaluation against clinically relevant pathogens.

Title: Exploring naringenin-clozapine combination for synergistic antipsychotic action: An in-silico study
Author: Nikita Arora|Pammi Gauba|Shweta Dang
Abstract: Naringenin has natural origins with reported antioxidant and neuromodulator properties, and clozapine is a prominent atypical antipsychotic with known dopaminergic and serotonergic mechanisms. Through molecular docking studies, interaction profiling, hydrophobicity analysis, ADMET simulation, toxicity prediction, and protein-protein interaction studies, a combined in-silico strategy was applied for the assessment of the ligand combination Clozapine-Naringenin on Dopamine D2 (DRD2) and Serotonin 5-HT2A (HTR2A) receptors. The two ligands moderately docked into the DRD2 and HTR2A receptor binding pockets with a binding energy of –7.5 kcal/mol and –9.9 kcal/mol respectively, strongly suggesting the ligands' ability to stably interact and reside in the two GPCR binding pockets. Hydrogen bonding interactions were strongly evident between Tyr370, Asn363, and Ser181 in HTR2A and between Arg1096 and Tyr1088 in DRD2. In addition, hydrophobic and π-alkyl interactions were evident and widespread. The characteristic seven-helix structure for all GPCR proteins was supported by hydrophobicity studies, giving credit to the validity and authenticity of the structure for both proteins. As per the model predictions from Swiss-ADME, the compound exhibits excellent oral and overall drug-likeness but has restricted blood-brain barrier penetration with considerable inhibition of CYP enzymes; this indicates possible PK interactions. It belongs to GHS class 4 with an LD50 value of 517 mg/kg. DRD2 and HTR2A were found to be the major signaling hotspots according to protein interaction network study. The Clozapine - Naringenin drug combination is a promising multi-target molecule.

Title: The molecular characterization of native plant growth-promoting bacteria of petrochemical-degraded soil for use as a soil conditioner
Author: Anshika Bajpai|Indira P. Sarethy
Abstract: Industrial activities are a significant environmental problem because of their degradation effects, which are associated with the reduction of soil productivity, microbial diversity, and the sustainability of ecosystems. Degraded soils can be restored to promote sustainable agriculture and the recovery of ecosystems, which contribute to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 2 (Zero Hunger) and 15 (Life on Land). Soil conditioners are needed as microbial-based remediation approaches are less effective at reducing contaminants and increasing soil biological functions. The objective of the study was to evaluate the soil physicochemical properties and to isolate the native bacteria with plant growth-promoting (PGP) activity. The physicochemical properties of soil samples collected from four industrially impacted places were analyzed, followed by bacterial isolation, purification, and characterization based on colony morphology and Gram staining from the selected soil sample. The isolates were tested for the production of phosphate-solubilizing, indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), total antioxidant capacity (TAC), and exopolysaccharide (EPS) production. The selected isolates were identified by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and phylogenetic analysis. A total of 20 different bacterial isolates were isolated, and there was a significant difference (p ≤ 0.05) in TAC and IAA production. PEC018 exhibited the highest activity of TAC (2735.88 µg AAE/gm) while PEC019 exhibited the maximum activity of IAA (22063.95 µg/gm). There were 13 and 12 isolates found to be able to solubilize phosphate and produce EPS, respectively. The molecular identification confirmed Priestia megaterium (PEC008), Lysinibacillus varians (PEC019), Lysinibacillus sphaericus (PEC001), and Rhodococcus ruber (PEC018). These are native multifunctional strains with potential for use as microbial soil conditioners.

Title: Novel therapeutic inhibitor targeting dysregulated kinase signaling in tau-mediated neurodegeneration
Author: Shravya Sharma|Manisha Singh
Abstract: In the case of tauopathies (like Alzheimer's disease), there is a progressive deterioration of neurons in association with abnormal tau hyperphosphorylation followed by destabilization of microtubules and the formation of neurofibrillary tangles. A variety of dysregulated kinase signaling pathways have been heavily implicated in the regulation of tau phosphorylation and disease progression, such as those involving glycogen synthase kinase 3β (GSK 3β), cyclin dependent kinase 5 (CDK5) and mitogen activated protein kinases (MAPKs). In this context, the MAPK/ERK signaling pathway, in particular ERK1/2, has been identified as a key pathway involved in regulating tau-associated processes, neuronal plasticity and survival and is of particular interest in Tau mediated neurodegeneration. In this review, the molecular mechanisms and the connection between kinase regulation, synaptic dysfunction and tau pathology are discussed, especially with regard to ERK1/2-mediated signaling. Previous studies have shown that HEK1/2 modulation can be implicated in tau phosphorylation pathways and has implications as a therapeutic target. Further, preclinical studies using natural compounds like Baicalein have been conducted to show their possible neuroprotective effects, but they need to be further tested in experiments to confirm their efficacy, target engagement and therapeutic relevance in tauopathies. In general, this review emphasizes the roles of kinase signaling pathways in tau mediated neurodegeneration and suggests ERK1/2 as an interesting therapeutic target. Additional in vitro, in vivo and clinical research is needed to assess the translatability of ERK1/2 targeting strategies for disease modifying treatment in tauopathies.

Title: Phenyllactic Acid from Saccharomyces boulardii Modulates EGFR & CXCR4: A Network Pharmacology & Molecular Dynamics Study
Author: Aarika Jain|Raj Kumar|S. M. Reddy|Jata Shankar
Abstract: Saccharomyces boulardii is a probiotic yeast widely used for managing gastrointestinal disorders such as irritable bowel disease and antibiotic-associated diarrhea. Bioactive compounds derived from S. boulardii exhibit anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and intestinal barrier-protective properties. However, the role of bioactive compounds in management of cancer remains unexplored. Using network pharmacology and molecular modeling, 116 bioactive compounds retrieved from literature, were analyzed. Gene targets of shortlisted 9 compounds through ADMET criteria were analyzed via protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks, Gene Ontology, KEGG, and Reactome enrichment. Protein-ligand interactions were evaluated through molecular docking. Complex stability was assessed using 50 ns molecular dynamics simulations followed by MM/PBSA binding free energy calculations. A total of 115 overlapping targets associated with gastrointestinal, neurological, and oncological disorders were identified. EGFR, STAT3, CTNNB1, and NFKB1 emerged as key hub proteins, with enrichment in PI3K-Akt, JAK-STAT, and PD-1/PD-L1 pathways. Phenyllactic acid was identified as the central metabolite through compound-target network analysis. Molecular docking and dynamics simulations confirmed stable binding of phenyllactic acid with EGFR and CXCR4, supported by consistent RMSD values (0.2-0.35 nm) and localized RMSF fluctuations. Key binding residues included Cys775, Thr790, Asp855, and Met766 for EGFR, and Trp94, Asp97, Tyr116, and Val112 for CXCR4. MM/PBSA calculations confirmed favourable binding energies of -26.2 kcal/mol and -24.6 kcal/mol for EGFR and CXCR4 respectively. Phenyllactic acid from S. boulardii acts as a multi-target modulator of EGFR and CXCR4, simultaneously influencing proliferative and migratory oncogenic signaling, warranting further experimental validation in cancer management.

Title: Thermodynamic profiling of the keratin-surfactant system using anionic surfactant for topical formulation
Author: Megha Mourya|Ashok Kumar Nadda|Poonam Sharma
Abstract: Keratin e xtracted from chicken feather biomass has been recognized as a sustainable biomaterial for pharmaceutical and cosmetic applications because of its biocompatibility and functional properties. In this study, the interactions between chicken feather-derived keratin and sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) were investigated in the temperature range of 25–40 °C using surface tension, contact angle, surface free energy, and thermodynamic analyses at different keratin concentrations of 1, 2, and 3% (w/v). Surface tension gradually decreased with increasing SDS concentration, indicating improved surface activity of the keratin–SDS system. The critical micelle concentration (CMC) increased from 0.0063 mM for 1% (w/v) keratin at 25 °C to 0.0105 mM for 3% (w/v) keratin at 40 °C, showing strong interactions between SDS molecules and keratin before micelle formation. The thermodynamic parameters confirmed that micellization was spontaneous, endothermic, and entropy-driven, with ΔG°ₘ ranging from −38.69 to −41.31 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔH°ₘ from 37.58 to 42.44 kJ mol⁻¹, and ΔS°ₘ from 255.95 to 267.56 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Moreover, the decrease in contact angle and increase in surface free energy show enhanced wettability and hydrophilicity of the keratin-surfactant system. Overall, these results highlight the potential of this system for stable topical formulations.

Title: Deciphering the Impact of Alginate and Biochar Immobilization on the Metals-Bioleaching Efficiency of Chromobacterium violaceum from Electronic Waste
Author: Tuba Khan|Parveen Kumar|Rajesh Kumar Sani|Sudhir Kumar
Abstract: Researchers have tried various immobilization methods (gel, nano particles etc.) for different applications (enzyme immobilization, catalysis, bioremediation, biosensing etc.), and among these microbes’ immobilization has also been tested by many groups. Here, in our case, the cyanogenic bacterium Chromobacterium violaceum has been immobilised on alginate and biochar to investigate the immobilization effect on overall bioleaching efficiency of metals from electronic waste. This study compared the bioleaching activities of free cells and immobilized cells entrapped in sodium alginate and sodium alginate-biochar matrices using printed circuit board (PCB) wastes as leaching material. Experiments of batch bioleaching were done under controlled conditions and the recovery of metal was monitored. Unlike the previously reported work by others, the free cells were found to have much higher leaching efficiency in comparison to the immobilized systems. Alginate beads were moderate in activity in the immobilized set ups and incorporation of biochar did not change or improve metal recovery. Free cells demonstrated the highest bioleaching performance, achieving copper, zinc, and nickel leaching efficiencies of 12.2%, 32.4%, and 18.8%, respectively. Biochar-alginate beads retained substantial copper leaching ability but showed markedly reduced zinc and nickel recovery, suggesting adsorption of released metals onto biochar surfaces. The low efficiency of immobilized systems is caused by diffusion limitations of the polymeric matrix, and hence restricted mass transfer of substrates, oxygen and metabolites. Also, biochar could have caused adsorption of washed-out metal ions or metabolic intermediates, further restricting measurable recovery. These results show a serious trade-off between the performance of bioleaching and the operational stability of immobilized systems. The present study offers useful mechanistic knowledge about the limitations of immobilized bioleaching systems, and it shows the need of optimized carrier design to overcome mass transfer limitations. The outputs can be used to rationally design effective and scalable bioleaching techniques to valorise e-waste.

Title: Explainable Deep Ensemble of Brain Tumor Classification based on MRI
Author: Anuj Gupta|Anita -|Manish Gupta
Abstract: Heterogeneity of cerebral neoplasms, loss of information labeling, and inter-class similarity make it difficult not only to differentiate the tumor clinically but also to establish separation of subtypes, taking Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) into consideration. It presents a neurotumor multiclass classifier, which has a probabilistic soft voting ensemble as the classification method, based on the transfer learning model using pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), using VGG16, ResNet50 and fine-tuned EfficientNetB0 as the basic classifiers. The experimental data is divided into four different categories: glioma, meningioma, pituitary and no visible tumor. The evaluation is carried out with the use of conventional performance indicators, which include recall, f1-score, confusion matrices, and a micro-averaged ROC analysis. Grad-CAM predicts clinical confidence and interpretability. The fine-tuned EfficientNetB0 model was found to have the highest test accuracy of 73.35%, compared to the equal-weight soft-voting ensemble with test accuracy 70.81%. The results indicate that the ensemble outperformed the ResNet50 and was marginally better than the VGG16, but still not better than the best EfficientNetB0 model. More frequent misclassification patterns, especially class confusion, are compared, and suggestions are made to enhance the sensitivity of the tumor.

Title: Ectomycorrhizal Diversity and Functional Metabolic Profiling Across Forest Disturbance Gradients: Implications for Ecosystem Restoration
Author: Avika Kaushik|Krishna Sundari Sattiraju
Abstract: Ectomycorrhizal fungi (ECM) play key roles in regulating forest ecosystem functioning as they are involved in nutrient uptake, seedling establishment, carbon allocation belowground and soil biological processes. Changes in vegetation structure, litter dynamics, soil chemistry, and forest disturbance gradients have a direct impact on the communities of soil fungi associated with the roots and their metabolic activities. Anthropogenic activities can alter ECM richness, the taxonomic composition of the Ecosystems, host associations, and enzyme activity. In relatively undisturbed forests, ECM communities are typically represented by taxonomically and functionally diverse groups of species, such as Russula, Lactarius, Cortinarius, Amanita, Tomentella, Inocybe, Boletus, Suillus , and Cenococcum lineages, while disturbed forests exhibited reduced diversity and increasing dominance of early-colonizing, ruderal, and stress-tolerant taxa such as: Laccaria laccata , Rhizopogon spp., Wilcoxina spp., Hebeloma spp., Thelephora terrestris, or Pisolithus tinctorius , depending on host and site conditions. The potential ecological impacts of these shifts include changes in nutrient cycling, production of extracellular enzymes, host colonization dynamics and direction of ecosystem recovery. However, based on recent developments in molecular ecology, fungal trait analysis, and functional metabolic profiling, the manuscript revealed that merely a shift in taxonomic composition is not enough to explain outcomes of post-disturbance ecosystems, and that community composition and metabolic capacity interact in ways that are important to resilience such information is crucial to designing restoration efforts in ECM-dominated forest lands.

Title: Salinity-induced dynamics in root system architecture of Brassica juncea : Insights from rhizovision explorer-based root phenotyping for climate-resilient agriculture
Author: Anurag Rawal|Krishna Sundari Sattiraju
Abstract: The salinity problem is still a major challenge in crop production in agricultural systems worldwide, yet the impact of salinity on crop root system architecture at trait level in Brassica juncea is still poorly known. The root architectural response is of special importance in the context of how mustard plants react to salt stress, as it is the first organ to be exposed. For this study, B. juncea seedlings were grown for 65 days under greenhouse conditions subjecting them to a range of NaCl concentrations (0, 12, 25, 50 and 100 mM). Root architectural features were quantified using RhizoVision Explorer, which has the ability to precisely image and quantify root complexity that would not be otherwise available in traditional studies. Unlike previous Brassica salinity studies that primarily focused overall root growth and physiological responses, this study comprehensively quantified multiple root architectural traits using RhizoVision Explorer to identify sensitive architectural indicators for salinity tolerance screening. It was observed that root architecture declined in a clear, concentration dependent manner with increasing salinity. One-way ANOVA revealed significant treatment effects on all measured root architectural traits (p < 0.001). At 100 mM NaCl, the root length and volume were reduced by 38.4% and 37.5%, respectively, compared with the control. Notably, lateral root growth and network area both dropped more than 50% at the highest salt concentration, indicating that lateral root growth and network area are much more sensitive to salt stress than total root mass. Pearson correlation analysis verified that all the measured traits decreased together, and the PCA accounted for 90.5% of the total variance in two components and showed a good spatial distinction between treatments of low and high salinity. Combined, these results indicate that salinity first systematically compromises the branching ability of the root system and then its explorative network in a non-random manner. The root tips and network area covered by roots were observed to be useful as early indicators of salt-induced architectural damage for salinity tolerance screening. Thus the findings demonstrate that root tips and network area can serve as rapid phenotyping traits for screening salinity-tolerant Brassica genotypes and may support breeding programs aimed at developing climate-resilient mustard cultivars for saline environments.

Title: A Bacteriophage Producing Lytic Plaques on a Multi-antibiotic selected Isolate from the Yamuna River
Author: A.C. Varshney|Sarethy P. Varshney
Abstract: The Yamuna River is heavily influenced by anthropogenic activities that contribute to the existence of antibiotic tolerant bacteria and their associated bacteriophages. However, bacteriophages associated with bacterial populations selected under multi-antibiotic pressure in the Yamuna River remain relatively unexplored. In this study, bacterial isolates were recovered from river water collected at the Okhla Barrage, Yamuna River, following selection with a combination of ampicillin, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline, and gentamycin. This approach resulted in the isolation of ten bacterial strains, among which isolate YAB-2 was selected for bacteriophage screening. Phages producing lytic plaques on YAB-2 were recovered and evaluated using the double agar overlay plaque assay. Circular, clear plaques were observed, with a phage titer of (6.5 ± 0.7) x 10 2 PFU/ml. Molecular identification of YAB-2 based on 16s rRNA gene sequencing and phylogenetic analysis identified the isolate as Klebsiella sp., showing 99.71% sequence similarity to reference strains. The recovery of phages capable of producing lytic plaques on YAB-2 provides culture-based evidence of phage-host interactions involving a bacterial isolate selected under multi-antibiotic pressure in the Yamuna River. These findings highlight the occurrence of environmentally derived phages associated with antibiotic-selected bacterial populations and provide a basis for further investigation of their host range, genomic characteristics, and potential applications in controlling antibiotic resistant bacteria. This study contributes to Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3 (Good Health and Well Being) by improving the understanding of various methods to combat antibiotic resistant bacteria and supports SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation) by examining microbial interactions in polluted river systems.

Title: Targeting ECM Remodeling through MMP Inhibition: Phytochemical Screening and Evaluation of Indian Medicinal Plants
Author: Ritika|Pammi Gauba|Vibha Rani
Abstract: The Extracellular Matrix (ECM) is an intricate network that serves as a crucial regulator for maintaining tissue stability and regulating the functions of cells. Abnormal ECM remodeling induced by the activities of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) is implicated in numerous diseases such as cancer, fibrosis, and health issues. Inhibition of ECM remodeling induced by MMPs thus emerges as an innovative therapeutic target. As such, the potential therapeutic effects of Traditional Indian botanicals, which have been known for presence of abundant phytochemical constituents, provide a promising solution for targeting these processes. In this study, the focus will be made on the identification of potential anti-MMP properties of Indian medicinal plants through phytochemical profiling and evaluation. Various plant extracts were prepared and assessed quantitatively for the content of phenolics (Total Phenolic Content) TPC and flavonoids (Total Flavonoid Content) TFC. Antioxidant activity was assessed using the DPPH free radical scavenging assay, a widely used method for evaluating the ability of plant extracts to neutralize reactive molecules associated with oxidative stress. Results indicated that selected medicinal plants contained significant amounts of phenolics and flavonoid compounds. The extracts with a higher concentration of these phytochemicals had higher antioxidant activity. The antioxidant capacity of various plants was investigated and the outcomes indicated that the plants contained useful quantities of phenols and flavonoids, so they could have the ability to protect biological systems from harm by free radicals and keep the integrity of the extracellular matrix. Overall, a positive correlation was observed between the levels of these phytochemicals in the extracts and their antioxidant activity. The Activity observed as free radical scavenging indicates that these plants have a high antioxidant potential, which is a potentially protective activity against the oxidative damage of biological systems and/or maintaining the integrity of the ECM. This could lead to modulation of ECM remodeling. In conclusion, this work demonstrates the promising role of Indian medicinal plants as natural ECM regulators. Combining phytochemical testing and antioxidative property assessment adds to the scientific credibility of this research and can help develop new plant-based functional products against ECM-associated diseases.

Title: Comprehensive Genome-Wide Analysis of the Starch Synthase Gene Family in Finger Millet ( Eleusine coracana )
Author: Vaishali Singh|Ankisha Vijay|Pooja Choudhary
Abstract: Finger millet is a nutritious cereal grain known for its health-related starch components and environmental flexibility. The starch synthases play an important role in starch synthesis because they control amylose and amylopectin production. The genome-wide investigation of the starch synthase (EcSS) gene family in finger millet was carried out using an in silico technique. Sixteen EcSSs were discovered and classified into five subgroups based on sequence similarities: SS1, SS2, SS3, SS4, and GBSSI. Protein architectures differed in terms of physicochemical characteristics and subcellular distribution; nonetheless, the majority of EcSSs were found in the chloroplast. Consequence motifs and domain analysis revealed the presence of catalytic domains related to the function of glycosyltransferases in starch synthesis. Chromosomal location and synteny analysis implied the expansion of the EcSS gene family due to duplication in evolution. The results of Ka/Ks analysis showed that most duplicated gene pairs were under purifying selection pressure due to functional constraints. Promoter analysis found various cis-acting elements responding to stress, hormones, and light conditions, indicating the involvement of the EcSS genes in both starch metabolism and stress tolerance. Overall, this study elucidates EcSS evolution and function, supporting future starch improvement in finger millet.

Title: Untargeted Metabolomics Profiling of the Fermented Broth of a Heritage Rice Variety
Author: Mahima|Indira P. Sarethy
Abstract: Fermentation is a well-established bioprocess which aids in improving the nutritional qualities, functional characteristics and bioavailability of cereal containing foods. Kalanamak rice is a traditional aromatic Indian variety valued for its distinctive fragrance and nutritional qualities; however, the biochemical changes occurring during its fermentation remain poorly understood. In this research, a Kalanamak rice broth with a rice-to-water ratio of 1:10 was fermented for 12 hours and then analyzed for total antioxidant capacity (TAC); antimicrobial activity; and metabolomic profile using an untargeted liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS) approach. After fermentation, TAC increased significantly, from 0.07 mg AAE/mL (unfermented broth) to 0.29 mg AAE/mL (fermented broth) (one-way ANOVA, p < 0.001). In total, 303 metabolite feature peaks were detected using the untargeted LC–MS and 209 unique metabolite candidates in seven major chemical classes were established. Polyphenols were found to be the major group of metabolites, followed by tetrapenes/ terpenoids, nitrogen containing compounds, and polyphenol derivatives. Several of the tentatively identified compounds are recognised for their antioxidant properties. Other metabolites identified contained antimicrobial properties but when tested against various microorganisms did not display any measureable bacterial inhibiting activity. This study represents, to our knowledge, the first use of (LC-MS)-based metabolomic techniques to characterize fermented Kalanamak rice broth, and can serve as a basis to establish the use of Kalanamak rice as a source of bioactive metabolites for the development of functional foods.

Title: In silico identification of edible mushroom-derived dual cholinesterase inhibitors as potential therapeutic candidates for Alzheimer's Disease
Author: Shehriz Khan|M. Udayabanu|Tiratha Raj Singh
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder and accounts for approximately 60–70% of dementia cases worldwide. It is characterized by progressive memory impairment, cognitive decline, and neuronal loss. Cholinergic dysfunction, resulting from elevated activities of acetylcholinesterase (AChE) and butyrylcholinesterase (BuChE), reduces acetylcholine (ACh) levels and contributes significantly to AD progression. Recent studies have highlighted edible mushrooms as rich sources of bioactive compounds possessing neuroprotective, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory properties that may support brain health and modulate cholinergic activity. The present study aimed to identify potential mushroom-derived cholinesterase inhibitors using an in-silico screening approach. Twenty-one bioactive metabolites from edible mushrooms were evaluated against AChE (PDB ID: 7E3H) and BuChE (PDB ID: 4BDS) using molecular docking performed with AutoDock 4.2.6. Protein–ligand interactions were further analyzed using UCSF Chimera and BIOVIA Discovery Studio. Among the screened compounds, ergosterol peroxide derived from Inonotus obliquus and ergosterol from Agaricus bisporus exhibited the strongest binding affinities toward both target enzymes, with docking scores ranging from −12.75 to −8.95 kcal/mol and favorable inhibition constants. Interaction analyses revealed stable binding within the catalytic pockets of AChE and BuChE, suggesting their potential as dual cholinesterase inhibitors. These findings indicate that mushroom-derived sterols may serve as promising lead compounds for the development of novel therapeutics against AD. However, further validation through molecular dynamics simulations, in vitro assays, and in vivo studies is necessary to confirm their efficacy, stability, and therapeutic potential.

Title: Microplastics in the Environment: Integrated Perspectives on Sources, Ecological Risks, Degradation Pathways, and Sustainable Management
Author: Anchal Tripathi|Anjali Rajput|Vikas Sharma|Ankisha Vijay
Abstract: Microplastics (MPs) are one of the emerging contaminants(ECs), which are produced wide range of human activities, and due to their persistence, bioaccumulation and toxicity they increasingly threaten the environment and have a negative impact on human health. This review presents the available literature regarding sources and classification of MPs, as well as their presence in terrestrial, freshwater and marine environments. Toxicity to aquatic organisms and as well as humans is also discussed , with special emphasis on the potential for ingestion, bioaccumulation and disruption of ecological functions. Special attention is given to the degradation of MPs by abiotic processes, such as photodegradation, thermodegradation, chemical degradation and advanced oxidation processes, and by biotic processes, such as bacteria, fungi and microalgae. In addition, recent developments in the treatment technologies of MPs and the existing global policies and strategies for plastic waste management are discussed. This review compiles recent knowledge on sources, environmental impacts, degradation mechanisms, treatment methods and regulations concerning MP pollution, giving a holistic overview of sustainable strategies to alleviate its impacts.

Title: Synthesis of Polymer-Coated Lutein Particles for Therapeutic Applications
Author: Kriti Sharma|Ashok Kumar Nadda
Abstract: Lutein is one of the naturally occurring carotenoids with strong anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and neuroprotective properties. This bioactive plant chemical plays a vital role in photoprotction from light and oxidative substances, as well as helping to maintain the structure and functionality of cell membranes, enabling it to perform vital physiological functions. However, because of its lipophilicity and decreased stability from its conjugated double bonds, it has limited bioavailability, poor aqueous solubility, and low stability, which pose significant challenges for clinical applications. The synthesis and characterization of lutein nanoparticles are covered in the current study. A polymer, stabilizer, and crosslinking agent are used to synthesize the lutein-loaded nanoparticles. The produced nanoparticles have shown high encapsulation efficiency (91.14±0.5%) and the lutein drug loading of ≈50%. Furthermore, Thermal analysis through DSC, TG, and DTG showed no thermal changes in lutein nanoparticles till the temperature of 280.4 °C, while the weight loss was 33.13% with the residue mass of 66.87% at 280.4 °C. The DTG thermogram exhibited several overlapping degradation peaks, indicating that thermal decomposition of the lutein nanoparticles proceeded through a multistep mechanism. The results present a platform for the development of lutein-loaded polymeric particles with increased thermal stability and drug loading capability.

Title: Android Malware Detection via Hybrid Static-Dynamic Analysis and Metaheuristic Feature Selection
Author: Kshamta Chauhan|Ekta Gandotra
Abstract: The rapid proliferation of Android applications has significantly increased the exposure of mobile devices to malware, necessitating accurate and robust detection mechanisms. While hybrid malware analysis that combines static and dynamic features has been widely adopted for Android malware detection, the effectiveness of such systems strongly depends on the selection of discriminative features. In this study, we present a systematic optimization and comparative evaluation of metaheuristic feature selection techniques within a hybrid malware analysis framework. Specifically, three metaheuristic feature selection algorithms, namely particle swarm optimization, genetic algorithm, and bat algorithm, are employed to identify the most relevant and discriminative set of features while minimizing redundancy and boosting the accuracy. An extensive set of experiments is carried out on a self-created dataset of Android applications to assess the effectiveness of the suggested approach. To further validate its effectiveness and generalizability, experiments are also performed on a benchmark dataset of Android malware. Five machine learning and three deep learning algorithms are trained with original features and the features selected using optimization algorithms for static, dynamic, and hybrid analysis approaches. Experimental results demonstrate that metaheuristic-based feature optimization consistently improves detection accuracy compared to non-optimized hybrid feature sets. According to experimental results, a gated recurrent unit constructed with features derived from the bat optimization approach for hybrid analysis gives the highest accuracy of 99.45%.

Title: GDSL Lipases as Regulators of Lipid Rancidity in Millet
Author: Astha Dumka|Pooja Choudhary
Abstract: Post-harvest rancidity substantially limits the quality and storage stability of pearl millet flour. Although triacylglycerol lipases have been associated with rancidity-related lipid degradation, the broader GDSL esterase/lipase family has not been systematically characterized in pearl millet. This study therefore aimed to identify and characterize GDSL esterase/lipase genes in the pearl millet accession PI583800 and to assess their potential relevance to lipid metabolism and rancidity-associated stress response. A genome-wide analysis identified 84 non-redundant PgGELP genes containing conserved GDSL lipase/esterase domains. Motif and gene-structure analyses revealed a conserved GDSL scaffold accompanied by substantial variation in motif organization and exon-intron structure, indicating possible functional diversification. The genes were unevenly distributed across the seven pearl millet chromosomes and scaffold regions, with prominent clustering on chromosomes 3 and 6. Promoter regions contained numerous hormone- and stress-responsive cis-elements, including ABRE, MeJA-responsive elements, W-box, MYB, MYC DRE, LTR and ARE motifs. Comparative synteny showed greater conservation with grass species, particularly Sorghum bicolor , than with Arabidopsis thaliana . In addition, several PgGELP transcripts were predicted to be regulated by miRNAs, with PgGELP78 identified as a putative miR164a target across the analysed species. This study provides the first comprehensive genomic framework for the pearl millet GDSL esterase/lipase family and identifies candidate genes for future functional investigation of lipid hydrolysis, stress responses and flour rancidity.

Title: Pretreatment techniques for digestate derived from a single-stage biogas digester
Author: Manisha Thakur|Ashish Kumar|Sudhir Kumar
Abstract: Food waste is one of the most common types of organic waste generated across the world, with an estimated amount of 1.05 billion tons, and managing it effectively continues to be a major environmental challenge. Anaerobic digestion (AD) has emerged as the most promising technology to turn waste into energy by converting organic waste into biogas and nutrient-rich digestate. The liquid fraction of the digestate has a high concentration of suspended, dissolved, and organic solids, which may restrict its efficiency and wider application. In the present study, the food waste digestate was obtained from a single-stage 1 m 3 biogas digester located at the Jaypee University of Information Technology, Solan, Himachal Pradesh campus. The efficacy of physical and chemical pretreatment methods with particular focus on coagulation-flocculation to improve the quality of digestate was evaluated. A comparative assessment of alum and ferric chloride for digestate clarification was performed based on treatment performance and cost-effectiveness. The study findings indicate that, at an optimum dose of 5000 mg/L, alum achieved the highest turbidity removal efficiency of approximately 93%, whereas ferric chloride achieved only 44% removal at an optimum dose of 1000 mg/L. Both coagulants achieved moderate volatile solids removal efficiencies of 37-39%. Alum was found to be more cost-effective due to its low cost (₹15/kg), improved clarity performance, and wider effective dosage range, even though ferric chloride required a lower treatment cost (₹55/m³). The implementation of proposed pretreatment techniques can be a sustainable and cost-effective strategy for lowering dependence on chemical-based fertilizers and supporting the circular economy.

Title: Phytochemical characterization and toxicological evaluation of ethanolic leaf extracts of Nerium oleander in Drosophila melanogaster
Author: Anoushka Bansal|Vibha Rani|Sujata Mohanty
Abstract: The increasing resistance to synthetic pesticides and their harmful environmental effects have highlighted the need for safer, eco-friendly alternatives. In this context, the present study evaluates the biopesticide activity of Nerium oleander , a plant known an ornamental plant abundantly found in the Mediterranean areas of Europe, North Africa, and Southwest Asia. A significant reduction in survivability accompanied by increased mortality was observed following exposure to the extract, indicating a concentration-dependent toxic effects likely to be associated due to insecticidal phyto compounds of N. oleander .
